# Abundant Energy (policy document)

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date  September 2026

Policy  Abundant Energy

Document Type  Policy Overview

Abundant Energy
In brief - New Zealand is an energy-rich country that
behaves as though we are energy-poor.

We have some of the best solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal resources in the world. But
we spend over $20 billion a year buying expensive fossil fuels to burn. And we still live
with volatile power prices, kids going to bed cold and Kiwi businesses leaving their
machinery idle or shutting up shop altogether.

At Opportunity we know we can do better.We can have abundant clean energy to power
warm comfortable homes and thriving businesses.

We will work across Parliament to secure a bold long-term plan to:

- Grow total generation capacity to 30 Gigawatts by 2050, about 2.7 times what we
have today.
- Reform the market to make sure generators and distributors are making the big
investments needed to power our energy future and putting the needs of
consumers first
- Support Kiwis to electrify our homes, communities and businesses

This is an investment in lower household bills, more manufacturing, higher wages, better
health, and a safer climate.

Opportunity Party | Abundant Energy  Page 1

---

Our reforms will:

- Change how our electricity market works so it incentivises new renewable
capacity and delivers lower prices for all.
- Invest in smart distribution networks to get clean energy where it needs to go
- Add at least 19 GW of new renewable generation capacity to the grid by 2050 to
reach a 30GW energy capacity target
- Electrify our homes and transport to make New Zealand the world’s most energy
efficient country

The Abundant Energy policy pillars

1. Boost Renewable Generation
New Zealand’s current electricity system is not set up for the energy future Kiwis
deserve. Decarbonisation will sharply increase electricity demand, as will adding new
industries like data centres, high tech manufacturing and green hydrogen, electricity
demand could more than double.

1.1 An Ambitious Long Term Strategy

Transpower’s “Accelerated Electrification” scenario envisages roughly 22 GW of capacity
by 2050. That may be just enough to meet core electrification needs and muddle
through decarbonisation. It is not enough to deliver energy abundance.

Reaching a more ambitious target of 30GW total capacity by 2050 means building at
least 19.2 GW of new renewable and storage capacity. That means annually building and
connecting about 40% more than the 556 MW added in 2024. More of what we’ve
already been doing - sustained and accelerated.

Most importantly, building large-scale renewable generation will require significant
private investment over an extended period. And that requires certainty - no more
on-again off-again pumped hydro or LNG terminals. That’s why we’ll work across parties
to lock in a 25-year Energy Strategy.

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 2

---

1.2 A New Zealand Capacity Investment Scheme

A capacity investment scheme based on that in Australia will use competitive tenders to
award long-term government contracts that guarantee a minimum revenue for new
renewables and storage, while also sharing excess revenue with the government above a
“ceiling” wholesale price. The Australian scheme has already supported more than 18GW
of new generation and storage capacity and across its life will unlock more than $70
billion of investment.

To avoid over-reliance on government price guarantees and maintain market price
signals, the Capacity Investment Scheme will apply to the second decade of operation of
new generation.This will provide the certainty necessary to kickstart large-scale
investment - especially in riskier prospects such as initial offshore wind facilities and
generation or storage capacity in constrained regions. To promote greater competition
in the generation market, initial tender rounds will also be restricted to new entrant
generators.

1.3 Supporting industrial-process electrification

To maintain momentum in reducing industry carbon emissions, ring-fenced proceeds
from future emissions trading scheme auctions will fund a range of measures to support
industrial electrification projects. Among the available toolbox are energy savings
guarantees. These are the inverse of the capacity investment scheme above, and could
be used to “match” new large sources of electricity demand to new renewable capacity.
See our statement for more.

2. Make the market work for consumers
High power prices and ongoing reliance on fossil fuels don’t happen by accident. They
are the result of long-standing perverse incentives that mean we under-invest in our
energy infrastructure. We need to align the way our markets work to make sure that our
electricity generators, distributors and retailers are all working towards the energy future
we want to see.

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 3

---

2.1 Ringfencing government dividend revenue

Currently the single biggest beneficiary of high end-user energy prices is the
Government itself through the dividends it receives from its ownership stake in three of
the four big gentailers. That has meant that successive governments have been
incentivised not to modify the regulatory structures that give rise to these super-profits.
By ringfencing the proceeds of the Crown’s ownership of these assets we will remove
these incentives. That will also allow around $500 million per year to fund the energy
system transformation initiatives below.

2.2 A single regulator and permissive regulatory environment

Five different regulators, agencies, and ministries oversee energy, with overlapping
mandates and slow decision-making. This fragmentation causes inefficiency, delays, and
poor long-term planning. We will merge key functions of the Electricity Authority,
Commerce Commission (energy-related functions), MBIE energy policy, Energy
Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA), Gas Industry Company and relevant
transport-electrification functions into one modern energy regulator, and one Ministry
of Energy.

A national policy statement on electricity generation and distribution will make it easier
for new generation and transmission infrastructure to obtain resource consent and
avoid subsequent litigation. This will include large grid-scale generation and storage,
generation for direct commercial use and smaller distributed infrastructure in homes and
communities.

2.3 Consolidated management of distributors and reformed pricing rules

New Zealand's 29 fragmented electricity distribution businesses (EDBs) —ranging from
Vector (600,000+ customers) to Buller Electricity (<5,000 customers)—lack the scale to
efficiently manage the investment required for decarbonisation. The Commerce
Commission's regulatory approach has constrained kept capital investments below the
levels demanded in distributors’ own asset management plans. At the same time,
complex compliance burdens smaller distributors disproportionately.

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 4

---

Consolidating management of the 29 electricity distributors into 6 - 8 larger groupings
will give them the scale necessary to manage and invest in their infrastructure, while
retaining the local ownership that matters to many communities. Reformed revenue
rules for these newly consolidated distributors, as well as Transpower, will free up
substantial additional capital for grid upgrades and anticipatory grid investment;
building capacity before it is needed rather than in response to new supply or demand.

3. Electrify houses, communities, and businesses
3.1 Adopt Rewiring Aotearoa’s low-interest electrification loans as part of a national
Ratepayer Assistance Scheme administered by local government
The RAS builds on an established successful model used by councils to access credit via
the New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency (LGFA). Using the LGFA, councils
reduce borrowing costs while providing investors with a stable return on investment. It is
important to note that, because the loan is tied to the individual rateable property and
no one shareholder owns more than 20%, the debt from these loans will not appear on
the books of the councils, or central government.

3.2 Empower communities to take control of their energy futures
An energy abundant future also means empowering our communities to have a stake.
This can mean local initiatives to generate, distribute or store electricity as well as
increase energy efficiency or make use of energy differently. In addition to the benefits
of New Zealand citizens taking charge of their own energy future, community-level
energy initiatives help to increase the efficiency and resilience of our overall energy
system. Two funds will help directly support these local initiatives:
A community engagement fund will directly support activities where communities work
together with electricity distributors to ensure local initiatives are accommodated and
supported within the wider electricity grid
Government will directly co-invest in small-scale (up to 15 MW) community-owned
generation and storage initiatives

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 5

---

3.3 Expand the Warmer Kiwi Homes programme to support solar generation and
appliance electrification for low-income households
EECA has already been highly successful in delivering subsidised upgrades to insulation
and heating for large numbers of lower income households. But why not go the whole
way and at the same time upgrade appliances and install solar generation? Warmer Kiwi
Homes is funded to $99.7 million in 2026/27, and that appropriation is exhausted after
this year even though it formally runs to June 2028. We will re-fund it and double it, at
about $200 million a year, so it can support the full electrification of those households
that are unlikely to be able to realise its benefits on their own.

3.4 Electrify urban public transport
Electrifying our urban bus fleet makes good sense with extensive new generation
capacity coming online. A fully funded mandate to Councils to electrify by 2030 will be
fully centrally funded, including both charging infrastructure and fleet assets.
In addition to significant decarbonisation and air pollution benefits, there are likely to be
spillover benefits to building out capacity to service electrified heavy vehicle fleets;
paving the way for electrifying other significant components of the transport industry.

3.5 Encourage businesses to electrify their fleets
Electric vehicles make sense for business - they reduce ongoing fuel costs and are more
resilient to volatile global fuel prices. As intense users, businesses are also well placed to
benefit from the advantages over time of electric vehicle use. The commercial fleet is
also a significant portion of new vehicle purchases - with commercial EVs will be sold in
to the secondhand market. Accelerated depreciation and fringe benefit tax exemptions
for business electric vehicles worth up to $50,000 (or $75,000 for utes and vans) will
encourage businesses to upgrade their fleets to electric.

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 6

---

FAQs

How much will this cost?
The operational expenditure for implementing this plan will all come from the ringfenced
dividend revenue from the Government’s ownership stake in the gentailers; currently
around $500 million annually. This will take this funding away from core crown revenue,
so represents a direct cost that will need to be funded through other revenue sources;
like the land value tax.
This dividend revenue funds the costs associated with:
- Administering lending to Councils for the ratepayer assistance scheme and
low-interest electrification loans (approx. $6 million annually)
- Administering the capacity investment scheme (approx. $5 million annually)
- Direct support to communities and electricity distributors to work together to
enable greater distributed generation (approx. $10 million annually)
- Co-funding for small-scale community generation projects in isolated
communities, and the grid infrastructure necessary to accommodate them (up to
$25 million annually to support up to $500 million of capital expenditure)
- Warmer Kiwi Homes initiative expansion (approx. $200 million annually, being the
base programme re-funded from 2028/29 plus the expansion)
- Mandated electrification of bus fleets (up to $125 million annually to support up
to $2.5 billion of capital expenditure)
- Accelerate depreciation and fringe benefit tax exemptions for fleet electric
vehicles ($126 million initially)
In addition to the above costs, the Capacity Investment Scheme will represent a
contingent liability on the Government balance sheet. While its expected value is $0, as
it is designed never to have to be paid out, this still presents risk if power prices fall too
dramatically.

What about grid stability?
The main source of grid stability in our proposal comes from overbuilding renewables;
having more renewable capacity available than current grid needs. This means that
variable renewable sources like wind and solar can be used ahead of hydro. Leaving

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 7

---

water in the hydro dams provides a reserve of highly responsive generation capacity.
Additional geothermal and hydro capacity will add to this.
Distributed generation generation and storage at household and community level does
not address broader “dry year” stability issues, but builds overall grid resilience and could
enable some peak shifting. Grid-scale storage further supports peak-shifting.
Thermal generation will still be available as a backup option; but it will be used in true
emergency scenarios, rather than as a routine part of the generation mix.

Why don’t you support structural separation of the gentailers?
Structural separation is a lengthy and costly solution, and doesn’t address the core
issues in the electricity sector. The fundamental problem is the perverse structural
incentives that give rise to underinvestment in generation across the board. The
gentailers could undoubtedly do better, but they’re reasonably competitive with each
other at both the retail and generation ends of the market.

Do you support the current Government’s commitment to build a LNG import
terminal?
No. This locks us in to long-term reliance on imported LNG. In addition to the
environmental impacts, this puts us at the mercy of potentially volatile international
prices.

Opportunity Party | Smart on Crime  Page 8

## Full text (verbatim)

Date  August 2026

Policy  Affordable Housing

Document Type  Policy Overview

Affordable Housing
A home is security and stability — the place we build good,
productive lives from.

But our housing market is broken, with houses unaffordable
for many, unhealthy for some, and home ownership out of
reach for generations of Kiwis. It’s time to make houses places
to live again, not just investment vehicles.

In addition to costing more than 7 times the median income, some of our homes are causing
a serious public health problem. New Zealand has some of the worst rates of respiratory
disease and breathing difficulties in the OECD, caused by decades of underinvestment and
weak building standards. One in five Kiwis are trapped in cold, damp, and mouldy homes,
directly fuelling thousands of preventable childhood hospital admissions and contributing
to an estimated 1,600 winter deaths every single year. That is a cost we can not afford.

We need to permanently narrow the gap between wages and house prices by stabilising the
market while we lift incomes and we have to build better homes, a lot faster. Opportunity’s
Affordable Housing policy presents a plan to do just that: Faster, Better, Cheaper.

1.  Faster (Planning, Consenting & Systemic Pre‑Approval)
With over 1,000 disparate regional zones, developers face an administrative minefield.
Innovative pre-fabricated and off-site manufacturing methods are stalled by slow council
consent, localised design reviews, and endless Requests for Information. To build more and
better houses, Opportunity will:

- Build on the Planning Bill with a simplified set of only 10 national consistent zones.
These will cut red tape that holds back the higher density development we need, while
affording automatic protections for highly productive farmland, civic assets, heritage
buildings and nature reserves.
- Expand existing frameworks to ensure a truly centralised pre-approval system for
proven building products, off-site manufacturing (OSM), and modular pre-fabricated
systems. Once a system is certified at the national level, local territorial authorities
will be prohibited from issuing Requests for Information (RFIs) or requiring redundant
design reviews. This will reduce the need for building inspections, reducing costs and
delays.
- Modify the Unit Titles Act and other legislation to make it faster and easier to build a
more diverse mix of homes, including everything from home offices and shop fronts to
co-housing, housing co-ops, Papakāinga, and multi-generational homes.

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 1

---

2. Better (Quality, Climate & Social Incentives)
Our cold, damp, and mouldy housing stock triggers severe, chronic respiratory illnesses
like asthma, bronchiolitis, and rheumatic fever. This gives New Zealand some of the highest
hospital admission rates for lung disease in the developed world and places an immense,
preventable burden on our public healthcare system. To improve the quality of our housing
stock as well as expand it, Opportunity will:

- Expand the “Warmer Kiwi Homes” insulation and heating retrofit programme already
run very successfully by EECA to cover private rentals that meet other eligibility criteria.
Available retrofits will also expand to include, double glazing, solar and appliance
electrification. See our Abundant Energy policy for more.
- Refund 100% of the GST collected during construction directly back to the local
council for any new build that achieves strong environmental and build standards
(such as Homestar 6+ or Passive House frameworks with future ready EV or Solar
infrastructure). This revenue is ring-fenced to fund local infrastructure and expand
community housing. This has the added bonus of reducing costs at the local council
level, reducing pressure on rates.
- Raise the minimum standards in the existing Healthy Homes Standards for rental
properties over time.
- Transition the Building Code away from rigid compliance checklists and toward
performance-based energy modelling. This shifts the focus from minimum
compliance to actual performance, guaranteeing that all new builds remain healthy,
energy-efficient, and naturally self-cooling year-round without relying on expensive
mechanical air conditioning.

3. Cheaper (Finance and De-risking)
Residential construction is plagued by financial volatility, and has fallen well below demand.
When lending conditions tighten, private developers go under, skilled tradespeople flee to
Australia, and New Zealand is left with a chronic housing shortage.

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 2

---

Funding for community-led and affordable housing has traditionally been locked behind
a messy patchwork of disconnected government grants and loans. This lack of certainty
prevents Community Housing Providers (CHPs) from building multi-year development
pipelines, while centralised quotas fail to adapt to regional demands.

To expand the supply of affordable homes Opportunity will:

- Task Kāinga Ora with delivering a diverse mix of housing types tailored to regional
needs so that smaller towns can clear their housing waitlists entirely and ensure
everyone has a safe place to live.
- Take the ‘bust’ out of the residential construction sector with a ‘Crown Build
Guarantee’ to back reputable residential developments by providing pre-sale and
completion guarantees.
- Make the Housing Flexible Fund a permanent capital pipeline and upgrade it so that it
uses localised waitlist data to back projects that address specific regional deficits and
so that a dedicated share of the fund is reserved for affordable rentals, building the
crucial “missing middle” between state housing and private ownership.
- Turn local councils, Community Housing Providers and developers into active partners
in ending the housing shortage by expanding the Community Housing lending facility
to give councils, CHPs, iwi and reputable private builders direct access to low‑cost
Crown development finance when they are delivering affordable or social housing that
is clearly tailored to local communities’ needs
- Defer land value tax liabilities for land under development up to a limit of two years
and subject to interest payment. See our Tax Reset for more information on the Land
Value Tax.

Affordable Housing — Frequently Asked
Questions
How much will this cost?
The foundational, market-stabilising elements of this policy - such as the Crown Build
Guarantee underwriting scheme and our low-cost development loans - require no direct,
upfront cash from the budget. Instead, they are funded by issuing targeted Housing and
Climate Bonds, leveraging the Crown’s balance sheet as a contingent liability.
Additional annual operating costs of $311 million are made up of the following:

Element  Estimated Annual Cost  Notes

National Pre-Approval  $15 million  Costed against standard MBIE/Commerce Commission
Unit  unit setups. Covers national modular certification, factory
audits, and digital consenting templates. Becomes partially
self-funding over time via manufacturer certification fees.

Crown Build Guarantee &  $30 million  An underlying $500m revolving development fund sits on
Housing Fund  the Crown balance sheet and is capital-neutral (loans are
repaid). The $30m budget line represents a 3% annual risk
provision.

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 3

---

Element  Estimated Annual Cost  Notes

Council GST share  $266 million  We estimate renewed construction generating
approximately 44,000 new builds at a total cost of $12.6
billion generating $1.9 billion in GST. Assuming 14% meet
quality standards results in GST rebates of $266 million.

The Warmer Kiwi Homes expansion has already been costed as part of our Abundant
Energy policy.

How do national pre-approvals stop local council delays?
Currently, every builder has to prove the safety and compliance of their building systems
over and over again to every single local council across the country for each and every build,
leading to endless, repetitive Requests for Information (RFIs) and design reviews.
By scaling the use of systems such as the MultiProof framework, we take core design and
component certification out of the hands of local councils and handle it once at a national
level. This delivers two massive upgrades to our building system:

- Quality: By elevating complex technical sign-offs to a centralised national standard,
we ensure that innovative, high-performance building systems are evaluated by
the country’s top technical experts, not overstretched local council staff. Precision
manufacturing in a controlled factory environment inherently delivers superior quality,
tighter structural seals, and better thermal performance than building standard homes
on a muddy site out in the elements.
- Certainty: Currently a design approved in one district can be arbitrarily delayed
or rejected by a council inspector in another region. This unpredictability stops
companies from scaling up. National pre-approval gives off-site fabricators, banks, and
homebuyers certainty. If a system is certified once, it is legally valid everywhere. Banks
can lend with confidence, manufacturers can safely invest in advanced machinery, and
families get guaranteed, predictable move-in dates.

By restricting local councils to checking local site foundations and utility hookups, they
are barred from re-opening structural design files. This avoids months of administrative
delay, guarantees a higher-quality build, and provides the exact certainty the sector
needs to grow.

How are local councils incentivised to support housing under this plan?
Under the current system, local councils are penalised for growth; they have to fund
the expensive pipes, roads, and infrastructure for new housing, but central government
pockets all the GST and income tax revenue generated by that growth.

First, by refunding 100% of construction GST back to the local council for any build that
hits high environmental baselines, we provide local authorities with an immediate revenue
stream. This turns housing development from a financial liability into a powerful revenue
generator for local communities, allowing councils to comfortably invest in high-quality
social housing of their own.

Second, by giving councils low-cost development loans, we dramatically reduce their
financial risk.

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 4

---

Together, these policies reduce the local council workload, reducing pressure on rates
and providing local government with a new funding source to get on with the important
infrastructure investment that local ratepayers can’t afford to fund on their own.

How do the Citizens Income and Tax Reset change rent subsidies?
Under Opportunity’s Tax Reset, housing support is modernised to complement the financial
floor provided by the Citizens Income. Because renters benefit the most from the broader
tax reset, the structural need for emergency interventions will naturally decrease. However,
to ensure targeted housing stability, the Accommodation Supplement will be replaced by
the Housing Support Income (HSI) built on two fundamental pillars:

- Decoupled, Instant Support: HSI is available to everyone who rents, subject to a
raised income maximum that captures more middle-to-low-income Kiwis. To stop
landlords from swallowing the subsidy, renters only enter their address—not their rent
amount. Rates are set to regional maximums, breaking the direct link between state
support and rent inflation.
- Rental Bond Insurance: To eliminate the stressful cash deficits that occur when
moving, traditional cash bonds will be replaced by a low-cost, annual rental bond
insurance paid by the renter. Tenants will no longer have to wait to recover a cash bond
from a previous landlord just to fund a new one—a practice that forces many low-
income families into deep debt. This single shift drastically improves labour mobility
and reduces financial anxiety.

The Income-Related Rent Subsidy (IRRS) and Temporary Accommodation Support (TAS)
will be retained as essential, targeted backups. However, by removing the waiting lists and
approval friction through HSI, these systems will serve as a clean, efficient safety net rather
than a default crutch for a broken rental market.

Won’t lower house prices hurt everyday Kiwi homeowners?
Our goal isn’t to crash the market or penalise families who worked hard to buy a home,
especially those who bought at the peak of the market. Our goal is to restore balance.

For decades, runaway speculation has driven a massive, unsustainable wedge between
what everyday Kiwis earn and what a home costs. We need to remember what housing is
actually for: homes for people to live in, not an investment vehicle for people to retire on.

To fix this responsibly, we need to narrow that gap from both sides:

- Lifting Incomes and slowing growth: We want to see New Zealanders’ wages rise
faster while gently slowing down house price rises. House prices will still rise over time,
but by keeping that growth low and stable for several years, we allow real salaries to
catch up. This narrows the affordability gap without destabilising the economy.
- Rewarding work over speculation: Our broader Tax Reset is specifically designed
to cushion this transition. By introducing a Land Value Tax (LVT) to shift speculative
capital out of empty land, we are simultaneously delivering significant income tax cuts
along with our universal Citizens Income. This means the average working family will
keep substantially more of their hard-earned pay packet every single week, boosting
household financial security.
- Lowering the cost to build: Alongside our Next Economy policies, our focus is on
stripping out the unnecessary bureaucratic costs of delivering new housing. By

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 5

---

making construction faster and cheaper, we make it highly economic for property
owners and community providers to replace “old, cold, and mouldy” stock with “new,
warm, and dry” homes.

This is a multi-year, responsible transition. We are moving New Zealand away from an
economy fuelled by untaxed property speculation and into a high-wage, productive
economy where shelter is secure and hard work is actually rewarded.

What is the Housing Flexible Fund?
The Housing Flexible Fund is currently a year to year “trial” contestable fund designed to
support delivery of social housing and affordable rentals.

We are upgrading this fund to provide long-term, predictable financing for affordable
rentals, urban equity-share co-operatives, and whānau-led papakāinga. Turning this into
a permanent fixture allows Community Housing Providers (CHPs) and iwi to plan multi-
year build pipelines with absolute financial certainty, rather than surviving year to year on
disconnected government grants.

What is a Crown Build Guarantee and how does it work?
Residential construction in New Zealand is trapped in a boom-bust cycle. When the
economy slows down, banks tighten lending, private buyers pull back, developers go under,
and our skilled tradespeople flee to Australia. When the market recovers, we are left with a
severe housing shortage and no workforce left to build.

The Crown Build Guarantee permanently takes the “bust” out of the sector by using the
government’s balance sheet to underwrite reputable residential developments. The
Crown provides pre-sale and completion guarantees. By ensuring that these homes will
be finished and purchased, banks can safely lend to developers even during an economic
downturn. This keeps hammers swinging, maintains a steady supply of houses, and
protects our construction workforce from downsizing.

If the government steps in during a market bust, what is the mechanism for
stepping back during a boom?
The Crown Build Guarantee is designed to act as an automatic economic stabiliser, it scales
down naturally when the private market is healthy.

The guarantee is only triggered when private market pre-sales drop below the threshold
required for a project to secure commercial bank financing. During a housing boom, private
buyers are plentiful, developments hit their pre-sale targets easily on the open market, and
the Crown’s underwriting framework remains completely untouched. The government isn’t
replacing the private sector; we are simply setting a structural floor to ensure construction
never grinds to a halt.

How do national pre-approvals and off-site assembly actually lower costs and
drive productivity?
The New Zealand construction sector has a productivity problem because we treat almost
every house like a bespoke project, built outside in the rain, the same way we have for
hundreds of years.

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 6

---

By combining national pre-approvals with Off-Site Manufacturing (OSM), we unlock true
industrial scale:

- Time is money: Standardized pre-approvals mean that once a factory-built design or
modular component is certified nationally, local councils are barred from reopening
design files or triggering endless Requests for Information (RFIs). This slashes months
off the consenting timeline.
- Factory precision: Building in a controlled environment reduces material waste,
avoids weather delays, and guarantees tighter structural seals and superior thermal
performance.
- Sector certainty: When manufacturers know a design is legally valid anywhere in
New Zealand, they can confidently invest in advanced automation and machinery,
permanently driving down the per-square-meter cost of building.

Opportunity Party  Housing  Page 7

# Breakthrough Economy (policy overview)

## Full text (verbatim)

Date  July 2026

Policy  Breakthrough Economy

Document Type  Policy Overview

Breakthrough Economy
New Zealand’s economy is stuck in low gear. But we have the
talent, resources, and opportunity to shift up.

Our economy pays New Zealanders’ wages, funds our retirements and generates
tax revenue for essential public services. There is a reason our young people are
leaving for jobs in Australia: persistently higher economic growth across the ditch has
compounded into a 35% gap in per capita GDP.

But there are good and bad ways to grow the economy. Mining the conservation
estate and trawling our ocean-floors are short term solutions, and the economic,
social and environmental bills are coming due.

New Zealand has the potential to take another path. Modern, high-skill jobs in sectors
like research, software and high-tech manufacturing generate more economic value,
overcome our distance from major markets and offer better wages and conditions for
New Zealand workers. They also have far less of an impact on our environment, and in
many cases can contribute to solutions to improve it.

1.  Build New Zealand’s Innovation Engine
Just like starting a business, building the future economy New Zealanders deserve
will require us to invest: in the science, innovation and skills that breakthrough
companies need to thrive.

New Zealand spends only 1.5% of GDP on public and private research and
development—about the same as Poland and Turkey. The OECD average is 2.7% and
high-tech frontier nations spend upwards of 3%.

This leaves our businesses and overall economy less productive and means we
struggle to turn ideas into commercial products, productivity gains and high‑wage
jobs. Our export base remains stubbornly weighted towards volume‑driven physical
goods and dependent on fluctuating international prices for those goods. We need to
get serious about becoming a high-tech innovation-driven economy.

We are lucky to have a well-educated workforce that we already invest heavily in, but
many graduates head offshore to higher‑paying labour markets, often carrying large
student debt that makes it harder for them to return. There are also overseas skills we
need to harness.

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 1

---

1.1  Boost core science and technology transfer funding
At Opportunity we want a long term strategy to boost the level of R&D in New Zealand.
We will re-commit to the previous target of 2% of GDP (with at least 0.6% made up of
public science) within the next ten years. But we will also set a longer-term objective
of 3% of GDP by 2050 to match the high-tech frontier economies we want to emulate.

The Save Science Coalition estimates recent cuts to core science have totalled at
least $90 million in annual operational funding and have resulted in the loss of 550
science sector jobs. The Fellows of the Royal Society have identified $300 million in
total funding cuts. While enhanced focus on advanced technology is laudable, this
should not come at the expense of other research sectors, To get our core science
sector back on track we will:

- Restore funding cut as part of science sector reorganisation in 2024
- Further expand total science funding to meet inflation-adjusted 2018 levels, by
boosting the major contestable funds and creating a new early and mid-career
research support fund
- Ensure that future contestable research funds include the humanities and social
sciences
.
1.2 Tax credits for technology adoption
Our current R&D tax credits deliver good returns, but stop short of incentivising
companies to make the big investments needed to roll out cutting-edge technology
and don’t incentivise stronger cooperation between private and public researchers.
To bridge this gap we will introduce a new tax credit scheme.

It will allow claiming back as a tax credit up to 25% of the cost of rolling out high-tech
solutions such as AI and digital platforms, new plant and machinery and networked or
autonomous equipment.

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 2

---

1.3 Make polytechnics an engine for technology-driven growth
Polytechnics can be regional anchors for practical, job-focused training, as well as
working directly with businesses to solve technical problems, access new export
markets and disseminate scientific expertise. To unlock the potential of polytechs to
level-up our regional businesses we will:

- Restore the entirety of the baseline funding for Polytechs cut by the current
Government and direct this funding towards training focused on core business
skills such as market development, accessing export markets, managing
cashflow and accessing finance
- Bulk-fund polytechnics and public research organisations—up to $10,000 per
business enquiry - to work with real-world business problems
- Empower polytechs with a mandate to lead regional productivity growth,
including by acting as hubs for sector-level initiatives

1.4  Double funding to incubator, accelerator, and deep tech programmes as
well as young enterprise
Opportunity will double total Government funding to the start-up ecosystem,
including existing and new incubator and accelerator arrangements and the young
enterprise programme.

It appears that these programmes have been successful in crowding in private
investment and increasing the survival of start-ups and helping them grow, but the
monitoring and evaluation has been weak. We will closely evaluate the impact of
these programmes, and undertake a systematic review to prepare the ground for
possible further expansion.

1.5 Create a world-class environment for safe AI adoption
By robustly regulating AI and supporting widespread business adoption, we can seize
the productivity opportunity it affords. Our dedicated AI policy will provide more detail.

1.6 Forgive Loan Interest to Bring Kiwi Talent Home
We want to encourage young Kiwis to go offshore, get experience and build
connections. But we also want to bring all that back home and use it to drive the New
Zealand economy.

We will roll back student loan interest on up to 3 years spent overseas, for both
those newly graduating at present and those currently overseas. The roll back will
be applied at the end of loan repayment, and conditional on being resident in New
Zealand when the loan is repaid.

1.7 Agree a population policy for stable long-term immigration
Immigration can bring expertise, energy and capital to the New Zealand economy.
We need to attract the best and brightest globally to come and help us build a
breakthrough economy.

But immigration also needs to be accounted for in our investment in infrastructure,
planning and social programmes. It hasn’t in recent decades.

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 3

---

The solution is a long term population strategy. This will set out the population
outcomes we want in the long-term, with average net migration outcomes to match.
Businesses, unions, NGOs and ordinary New Zealanders should have a say in what the
future of our population looks like, but at Opportunity we think moderate sustained
positive migration is the way to go.

2. Stand up for consumers
New Zealand’s economy is increasingly shaped by sectors where a handful of large
companies dominate. In these concentrated markets, big incumbents enjoy scale,
political access, regulatory influence and weak competition law, which makes it hard
for new entrants to gain a foothold. Market concentration in banking, supermarkets
and building materials cost the average household $30 every single week. It also
suppresses productivity growth by reducing competitive pressure to innovate and
improve efficiency across our economy.

2.1 Strengthen Competition Law and Enforcement
New Zealand has one of the weakest competition regimes in the world. This has
enabled concentration and excessive profits in many critical business sectors such
as banking, supermarkets, insurance, building supplies, aviation and utilities. This
doesn’t just result in higher prices for consumers; it acts as a drag on the overall
economy. Smaller dynamic firms cannot get a foothold, or are themselves bled dry by
excessive costs.

To bring market competition back to the New Zealand economy, Opportunity will
strengthen the Commerce Commission’s powers and independence by enabling it to:

- Break up dominant companies where competition has clearly failed. The
Commerce Commission will be able to ask the High Court to order the sale of
assets, separate business operations, or require access to key infrastructure
when market power has become too concentrated and other remedies have
failed.

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 4

---

- Use an expanded toolbox to fix competition problems in industry-appropriate
ways, including industry-wide remedies following a market study or where
there is tacit collusion and binding commitments as part of market dominance
investigations.
- Proactively investigate industries where competition is weak. The Commerce
Commission will have greater freedom to launch investigations and market
studies where there are signs that consumers and smaller businesses are being
disadvantaged.

In addition, Opportunity will create a Consumer Advocacy Fund - a dedicated fund to
support independent consumer representation in major market reviews, regulatory
processes and competition investigations. This would help ensure consumers are
represented as effectively as large corporate interests.

Strong competition is one of the most effective ways to reduce prices, increase
innovation, lift productivity and improve living standards. These reforms would give
New Zealand a competition regime comparable to those found in many of the world’s
most productive small economies such as Denmark, Finland and Ireland.

3. Power up small business
Our economy is built on small businesses, and they have the potential to drive the
breakthrough economy. But they need support to address key skill and capability gaps.

Our current corporate form rules also mean that companies are driven to prioritise
profit above all else, while non-profit organisations and charities lack the business
models and structures to access finance for growth.

3.1 Get serious about supporting SMEs
Most SME operators—particularly sole traders and micro enterprises—are under-
capitalised, time-constrained and operationally focused.

To support SMEs more effectively, we will:

- Fund FinCap and the Building Financial Capability sector to provide simple
financial and accounting advice to small businesses. Many small businesses are
financially intertwined with their owner-operators, and household budgeting
needs can have business issues underlying them. Building capability among
budgeting services to meet this need is a practical way to improve the business
capabilities of small businesses and the New Zealanders who put their hearts and
souls into them.
- Review the ACC levy system with a view to introducing risk-weighted levies for
those engaged in multiple different work activities.
- Reverse the Retail Payment System (Ban on Merchant Surcharges) Amendment
Bill if passed, and review competition within our payment infrastructure generally.
- Make the R&D tax credit more accessible by introducing processing time
requirements and a special track with simplified compliance requirements
for spending below $250,000 and improving outreach and support to smaller

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 5

---

businesses, especially in high value manufacturing. Develop innovation access
programmes to enable smaller companies to participate in R&D as part of
consortia and alongside CRIs, universities and polytechs.

3.2 Structure for Purpose
There is a gap in New Zealand for a legal entity structure that both drives the
economic growth of a traditional for-profit company and delivers the social benefits
of a charitable organisation.

We will amend the Companies Act to establish a new legal structure: the Impact
Company. Similar structures already exist overseas including in the UK, Canada,
United States, and Italy.

To qualify as an Impact Company, a business will need to state an explicit social and/
or environmental purpose in its constitution and publish annual Impact Reports that
account for social and environmental outcomes.

To encourage growth in new impact sectors, we will also enable companies or
individuals that invest in Impact Companies to deduct the investment as they would a
donation to charity, up to a maximum of $100,000 annually.

4. Frequently Asked Questions
How much will this cost?
The total estimated cost to the Crown of this policy is $1.33 billion of additional annual

How can you claim to deliver additional annual GDP growth?
Predicting the growth impacts of policies is not straightforward. We estimate our
mix of policies could deliver up to 2% additional GDP growth on average over the long
term. Comparator small economies such as Singapore and Estonia have sustained
similarly high growth rates over multiple decades.

Productivity Unleashed and many of our other policies are in line with expert advice
from the likes of Treasury and the OECD on high impact pro-growth reforms for New
Zealand.

Our Abundant Energy policy will make energy prices for businesses both lower and
more stable, unlocking opportunities for a wide range of energy intensive businesses
such as data centres and manufacturing. Our Tax Reset policy will redirect significant
capital from unproductive housing investment and significantly increase our saving
rate over time. It will also work together with our Affordable Housing policy in the long
term to improve the functioning of our urban spaces and the businesses that operate
and grow within them.

Productivity Unleashed invests substantially in three areas that are repeatedly
cited by the OECD as drivers of New Zealand’s poor productivity and GDP growth
performance: innovation, competition and skills. Some indication of the impacts that
could be realised include the following:

- Government science spending is well-established to “crowd in” private spending
on R&D - enhancing its impact. Estimates of the total economic effect of
government science spending tend to come from larger OECD economies
with deeper capital pools and more R&D intensive industries compared to New
Zealand, but can range as high as a 3 - 4x multiplier.
- The impacts of better competition law and enforcement, even in jurisdictions like
New Zealand with relatively developed existing frameworks, is well established.
The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority summarises a range of this
evidence.
- MBIE analysis has looked at the economic impact of measures such as R&D and
commercialisation spending. It found the impact of the former Growth Grants
(similar to our proposed polytech funding arrangements) delivered an economic
multiplier of 1.22-3.65.
- A widely cited estimate for Denmark suggested a peak contribution to total factor
productivity growth from generative AI of up to 1.5%

What has the current government’s record on innovation been like?
The current government has moved in the wrong direction by cutting core Crown
science and innovation funding from a system already under strain. Budget 2024
removed hundreds of millions from the Science, Innovation and Technology portfolio.
It allowed inflation to erode baselines, wound up the National Science Challenges
programme, and cancelled future rounds of several key funds. Experts estimate this

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 8

---

has contributed to hundreds of job losses across universities and Crown Research
Institutes. These cuts weaken the pipeline from discovery science to commercial
innovation, reduce New Zealand’s capacity to respond to long‑term challenges like
climate change and biosecurity threats, and send the wrong signal to businesses the
very moment we need them to increase their own R&D investment.

Isn’t this a dramatic shakeup of our competition law?
Yes. We think the current state of competition in many business sectors warrants a
shakeup, rather than continued tinkering like the current Commerce Act Amendment
Bill before Parliament.

New Zealand’s competition regime is largely modelled on Australia’s and together we
are near-unique among developed nations in lacking robust remedies like the ability
to break up monopolies, impose industry-wide conduct obligations or address tacit
collusion. This has led directly to our near-unique market concentration and super-
profits.

Our proposal is modeled on provisions recently introduced in the EU and UK; both
regarded as highly effective competition regimes.

Why not break up the banks and supermarkets?
Opportunity is open to the concept of structural separation of industries like banking,
supermarkets and electricity generation. However structural separation is a blunt
instrument that always imposes significant costs and market disruption. We think it
should be done on the basis of expert analysis, and supervised by the Courts. In some
cases structural separation might be imposed, but more importantly, the threat of the
Commerce Commission using it will improve market behaviour across the board.

Giving the Commerce Commission the power to fight the monopolies in the High
Court means they can also go after the many other highly concentrated sectors that
don’t receive much political or media attention, but do impose significant costs on
New Zealand consumers.

Opportunity Party  Economy  Page 9

# Citizens' Voice (policy document)

> Archive note: Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; page furniture (headers/footers, page numbers) is kept as extracted; bullets normalised to Markdown and page breaks shown as horizontal rules. Layout, images, charts and tables-as-graphics are not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Date  June 2025

Policy  Citizen's Voice

Document Type  Policy Overview

Direct democracy
Right now, big decisions are often made without fully hearing
from the public—or only from the loudest or most powerful
voices. Polarisation, fueled by politicians from both sides,
makes it ever harder to find common ground. Many New
Zealanders feel alienated or demoralised by politics; political
participation is in long-term decline.

Our political system is also not well equipped to address long-term issues. Politicians
are naturally focused on the three-year electoral cycle. But the most important issues
for New Zealand are often longer term, like climate change, the impacts of an ageing
population or our constitutional future.

What if there were a way to ensure that New Zealanders had a direct voice in the big,
long-term decisions that will affect their lives most?

Opportunity will:

- Convene citizens assemblies to consider and advise on major issues
The citizens assembly will provide deep consideration of issues that are difficult
to navigate and impact New Zealand’s long-term future. The assembly will consist
of a broadly representative group recruited at random from across the country. It
will consider evidence from experts, interest groups and other citizens and make
recommendations that the Government must respond to.

- Appoint a Parliamentary Commissioner for Citizens’ Voice
This independent role will be responsible for enabling citizen participation in
solving the most important long-term issues for society. Like the Ombudsman,
the Commissioner will be appointed by Parliament, and will work independently
from both the government and Parliament. They will focus on what’s best for New
Zealand in the long term—not just what’s popular today.

- Use other tools for broad-based citizen participation
The Parliamentary Commissioner will also provide online and offline ways to
enable citizen participation tailored to the issue being considered. These could
include online surveys and digital deliberation tools as well as in-person public
forums and hui.

Opportunity Party  Direct Democracy  Page 1

---

What it means for you
- Better decisions: With broad input, policies are more likely to work and to gain
public support.
- A stronger democracy: This process ensures decisions are informed by the
people who live with their consequences.
- A way through intractable issues: Citizens assemblies can consider issues
that politicians are too scared to touch, or that have become too politicised for
reasonable debate, finding a way through the mire.
- A real voice: Whether through a survey, a workshop, or a forum, there will be
more ways to share your views on the issues that matter most.

This isn’t about replacing elections or Parliament. It’s about improving how decisions
are made, especially on big challenges that require long-term thinking and public
buy‑in.

Our representative democracy can struggle to address
long-term issues
Big decisions are typically made by politicians with advice from experts, pressure from
lobbyists and donors, or consultation that only reaches a limited audience. This can
lead to outcomes that prioritise immediate electoral prospects over the long-term.
Governments from both sides “kick the can down the road” on issues that will have
a massive impact on New Zealand but are too slow-moving to result in an immediate
crisis, or require solutions that cannot be implemented within one Parliamentary
term. Current examples include the housing crisis, climate change and the impacts of
our ageing population.

Opportunity Party  Direct Democracy  Page 2

---

Photo: Climate Assembly UK

Citizens assemblies can make better and more democratic
decisions
An assembly will have the same number of citizens as MPs in the current Parliament.
They will be randomly selected to be representative of New Zealand’s population. The
assembly will be guided by a suitably qualified facilitator and supported by politically
neutral, professional staff. Assembly meetings will take place using a mixture of in-
person and online formats. Given the complexity of the issues at stake, and the need
to build consensus, each assembly may last for up to a year.

The critical difference here is that recommendations will come directly from the
people involved in these processes, not from politicians, officials or experts, or
groups with vested interests. But the assembly won’t simply consider the issue based
on members’ knowledge. It will hear evidence from experts, interest groups and the
wider public, and can commission research.

Participatory decision-making will build consensus and public support
The process of making a decision can be as important as the decision itself. Citizens
coming together to debate and find solutions to big issues can help to build
consensus and deep support for agreed outcomes. It can also build a broader sense
of “buy-in” to democratic processes.

All documents the Citizens Assembly considers will be made public (with limited
exceptions to preserve the likes of privacy or commercial sensitivity) and, to
the greatest extent possible, proceedings will be open to the public and allow
opportunities for input in a variety of ways.

By contrast, current politics is leaving an increasing number of New Zealanders
feeling alienated and demoralised. Voter turnout at local and national elections
continues to slide and our political discourse – often online – is becoming ever more
polarised. Politicians from both sides take advantage of and fuel this polarisation.

The Treaty Principles Bill has highlighted this issue. The Bill itself is short-sighted and
deeply divisive. But there is a real need to have a national conversation about our
Constitutional arrangements, including the role of Te Tiriti. That conversation needs
to involve all New Zealanders – and most especially the two parties to the Treaty. It
has the potential to shape how we define ourselves as a nation for generations to
come – far too important an issue to leave to the politicians.

Opportunity Party  Direct Democracy  Page 3

---

A Parliamentary Commissioner will facilitate a wide range
of direct democratic participation
The Commissioner will oversee a range of public engagement processes, tailored to
the issue at hand. The Commissioner’s role is to ensure the process is fair, inclusive,
and well-informed – but the ideas and solutions are generated by the participants
themselves. The most important of these will be the citizens assemblies, but these
will be supported by a range of innovative tools to enable participation by a broad
range of citizens, facilitated by the Parliamentary Commissioner. These will include
public forums and hui as well as digital tools such as surveys and online deliberative
platforms.

For example, if Parliament wanted advice on how to provide affordable, accessible
healthcare, the Commissioner might gather public input through digital
platforms, community forums, and citizen panels to develop thoughtful, inclusive
recommendations.

Topic selection will promote democratic participation
Topics could be identified in several ways:

- Parliamentary Requests: Parliament could ask the Commissioner to focus on
specific challenges.
- Public Petitions: If enough people (for example 150,000 signatories) call for a
topic to be explored, it could trigger action.
- Independent Initiative: The Commissioner might identify critical issues based
on research or public discourse.
- Community Feedback: Input from iwi, community groups, or experts could
highlight pressing concerns.

The decision process will be transparent, with clear criteria focused on importance,
complexity, and public relevance.

Parliament will have to respond to citizens’
recommendations
Once a process is completed, recommendations will be submitted to Parliament,
which will be required to debate them and provide a formal response.

The Commissioner will monitor Parliament’s responses to recommendations, tracking
actions taken, and producing annual reports on the outcomes. These reports will be
made public to ensure transparency and accountability.

Opportunity Party  Direct Democracy  Page 4

# Clean Up Politics (policy document)

## Full text (verbatim)

Date  August 2026

Policy  Clean Up Politics

Document Type  Policy Overview

Clean Up Politics
Democracy means rule by the people. Clean Up Politics is
Opportunity’s plan to make sure the people of New Zealand
rule this country. Opportunity will hard-wire honesty,
transparency, and genuine public participation into our
democracy, so that corruption and the abuse of power cannot
take hold.

New Zealand has long prided itself on low corruption and high trust. But we can’t
assume that a historically clean political culture will always protect us. A recent
Serious Fraud Office assessment concluded that the risk of corruption is increasing,
incidents are under-reported and government agencies are insufficiently prepared to
prevent and respond to corrupt practices. New Zealand needs modern, world-leading
rules that keep pace with growing private and foreign influence in politics, expanding
political lobbying, and increasingly centralised executive power.

At present, New Zealand has no overall caps on political donations, and reporting
thresholds permit donors to pay significant sums to parties with limited transparency.
Lobbyists enjoy easy access to politicians. They have no register, no enforceable
code of conduct, and no obligation to disclose whom they meet or act for. New
Zealand has no central body responsible for addressing corruption. Transparency
International and local experts have repeatedly warned that these gaps create risks
and public perceptions of policy being ‘for sale’.

Opportunity will work across Parliament to lock in a bold, long-term package of
reforms built on three pillars.

Opportunity Party  Democracy  Page 1

---

1.  Regulate lobbying
Recent controversies have shown how difficult it can be for the public to see who
influences important government decisions, what interests they represent, and what
contact they have had with decision-makers. Opportunity will introduce a Political
Influence and Lobbying Bill that creates:

- A one-year cooling-off period closing the revolving door between Ministers,
senior staff and officials, and lobbying roles.
- A mandatory, public, searchable lobbying register, with quarterly disclosure of
who lobbied which office-holders, on what issues, for which clients.
- A statutory code of conduct for lobbyists, with sanctions from public censure to
deregistration and fines. The code will include:
- A prohibition on contingent‑fee arrangements for securing specific policy
outcomes or contracts;
- Requirements to avoid conflicts of interest among clients and declare
relevant financial interests;
- Transparency rules for communicating which clients they are working on
behalf of and what their objectives are;
- Requiring that all lobbying communications with Ministers concerning
official business be conducted through, copied to, or recorded in official
parliamentary systems so that they are retained and subject to the OIA;
- Confidentiality rules for dealing with client and government information.
- Foreign lobbying safeguards, with disclosure of foreign state or foreign-
controlled clients and heightened scrutiny of lobbying on critical infrastructure,
national security, media ownership, and strategic resources.

2. Reform political donations
New Zealanders believe money buys access and influence in politics. A 2020 Victoria
University of Wellington survey found 34% of the public believed corruption was
widespread throughout Government, and 71% had ‘not much’ or ‘little to no’ trust in
how political parties are funded. Opportunity will sever the link between donations
and influence, and make politics a competition of ideas, not fundraising machines.

- A $30,000 cap per donor per party per electoral cycle. The Independent Electoral
Review proposed an electoral donations cap at this level. Loan-as-donation
structures and pass-through arrangements will be banned.
- Only registered voters may donate. Opportunity will eliminate donations from
companies, trusts and other entities, and ban donations from anyone who is not
registered to vote in New Zealand.
- Lower disclosure limits. Opportunity will lower the public disclosure threshold to
$1,000 and require parties to publish audited annual statements.
- Spending limits across the full cycle. Party and candidate advertising spending
limits will apply across the full three-year electoral cycle, not just the final three
months, with the Electoral Commission publishing quarterly spending summaries.

Opportunity Party  Democracy  Page 2

---

3. An integrity system that works
Good rules mean little without institutions that enforce them. Opportunity will
establish a genuinely independent anti-corruption body with investigative,
prevention, and education functions, integrating and co-ordinating existing anti-
corruption responsibilities. It will cover the full range of public officials, including
Ministers, MPs, parliamentary staff, the public service, Crown entities, SOEs, local
government, and contractors performing public functions. Its responsibilities will
include:

- Investigating - including by compelling evidence and exercising search and
surveillance powers under judicial warrant - and exposing corruption. This will
include publicising findings as well as referring matters for prosecution to other
bodies such as the Serious Fraud Office or Police.
- Enforcing new rules that prohibit authorised electoral advertisements containing
statements of fact that are inaccurate and misleading to a material extent,
backed by the requirement to publish corrections.
- Monitoring and reporting on systemic risk of corruption overall within the public
service.
- Administering the lobbying rules described above.
- Educating the public sector on integrity and corruption
- Ensuring government entities have appropriate internal prevention and response
measures in place.

Alongside the anti-corruption body, Opportunity will upgrade the day-to-day integrity
rules:

- Official Information Act reform: narrower withholding grounds, strengthening
the public interest balancing test, enforceable timeframes for actually providing
documents and binding order-making powers for the Ombudsman.
- Stronger pecuniary interest rules: lower disclosure thresholds, mandatory
disclosure of beneficial interests in trusts, and real-time reporting of significant
changes.
- Better whistleblower protections, with broader coverage, safe channels to the
anti-corruption body and other enforcement bodies, and stronger protection
against retaliation.
- A stronger Electoral Commission with the funding and powers to enforce the
rules in real time.
- An independent policy costing unit available to all registered parties, to reduce
fiscal ‘spin wars’ and improve the quality of election debates.

Opportunity Party  Democracy  Page 3

## Full text (verbatim)

Date  September 2026

Policy  Climate Action

Document Type  Policy Overview

Climate Resilient Aotearoa
The decisions we make this decade will impact generations to
come.

Climate change is not a distant threat – it is reshaping New Zealand's weather, coastlines,
farms, and infrastructure. It is both a moral duty and an economic necessity to act:
cutting emissions at the source, preparing communities for the disruption already locked
in, and building enduring institutions that will hold governments to account across
political cycles.

In 2019 New Zealand showed what is possible when climate leadership rises above party
politics. Through sustained cooperation across left and right parties, Parliament forged
the broad consensus behind the Zero Carbon Act: establishing enduring emissions
targets, carbon budgets and an independent Climate Change Commission. Its
near-unanimous passage demonstrated that compromise is not weakness: it is how a
small democracy creates the certainty needed for households, businesses and
communities to plan for the future.

New Zealand must regain that commitment to concerted action. Climate policy cannot be
rewritten after every election or reduced to a contest between denial and disruption; it
must be ambitious, practical, fair and durable. We will work across political lines to restore
a shared national direction that cuts emissions efficiently, strengthens resilience and
gives every New Zealander confidence that the transition will be managed competently
and fairly.

---

1. Cut emissions and everyday costs. Together.
For too long, climate policy has been framed as a choice between reducing emissions and
protecting living standards. Opportunity rejects that false trade-off. New Zealand's path
to a low carbon, climate resilient future should be built around making households and
businesses more efficient, more resilient, and less exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices.

Homes

Electrifying our homes is not only a huge opportunity to reduce emissions but to reduce
electricity bills and improve health outcomes too.

- Ensure all rental properties comply with the Healthy Homes Standards and update
them to provide all residential tenants a right to charge EVs.
- Require all new builds to be wired to accommodate EV charging and solar.
- Allow building energy improvements (e.g. efficiency measures, rooftop solar and
batteries, two-way smart EV chargers) to be written off against tax.
- Adopt low-interest electrification loans as part of a national Ratepayer Assistance
Scheme administered by local government - as referenced in our Abundant Energy
policy.

Transport

Incentivising electrification of personal vehicles and public transport fleets drives more
investment in renewable energy generation and makes us less reliant on foreign fossil
fuels from a volatile global market.

- Remove fringe benefit tax and accelerate depreciation for electric vehicles to
accelerate the transition to an energy efficient fleet so that more new EVs enter
the country.
- Introduce sinking-lid tailpipe emissions standards for all newly imported vehicles.
- Electrify the urban bus fleet by 2030.
- Replace the public sector vehicle fleet with EVs (and hybrids, where justified) as
vehicles come up for renewal.

Industry

New Zealand businesses are acutely exposed to volatile international fossil fuel markets
and geopolitical shocks. Replacing coal and gas with renewable electricity and other
domestically produced low-emissions energy will strengthen energy security, reduce
price shocks, keep more investment in New Zealand, and give businesses more
predictable long-term costs.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 2

---

Opportunity will:

- Establish the Industry Energy Resilience Fund (IERF) to support industrial
decarbonisation, funded by a green bond raised against future ETS auction
revenue.
- The IERF will support businesses to transition away from fossil fuels by funding the
upfront capital for new equipment, grid connections or network upgrades. It will
use a range of financial instruments including concessional loans, energy savings
guarantees and loan underwriting, with grants reserved for targeted uses.
- Reverse the 2025 decision that cut the number of entities required to undertake
climate reporting from 164 to 76 and removed directors' liability, and expand the
Ministry for the Environment's Measuring Emissions Catalogue into a free national
dataset so small suppliers are not charged twice for the same data.

Agriculture

New Zealand's prosperity depends on maintaining access to premium global markets.
Increasingly, our markets and customers require credible farm data and emissions
information, and evidence of continuous improvement. Reductions in agricultural
emissions are possible, affordable and in the interests of our farmers and producers to
meet global demands.

Opportunity will:

- reward farmers for maintaining and enhancing biodiversity, wetlands, native
vegetation, riparian planting and other ecosystem services. See our Healthy Land
policy for more.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 3

---

- continue investment in agricultural science, technology development and
commercialisation as part of a thriving science sector. See our Breakthrough
Economy policy for more.
- explore a cap-and-trade market or levy structure for reducing the annual flow rate
of biogenic methane into the atmosphere in line with five year emissions budgets
and long-term targets.
- invite proposals for market-based systems for reducing nitrous oxide emissions
into the atmosphere.

2. Build our national climate resilience
Climate adaptation – planning for the disruption already locked in – is not optional.
Adaptation means getting ahead of damage instead of paying for it twice: first in disaster
clean-ups, then in higher insurance, higher rates, and broken infrastructure.

We are already seeing the early stages of insurance retreat: when insurers raise
premiums, restrict cover, or withdraw entirely from high-risk areas. This is not just an
insurance issue. It is a housing and infrastructure issue, a fairness issue, and a national
economic issue.

Resilient governance

Climate risk is harder to manage when information and responsibilities are unclear and
when we’re always on the back foot. Clear rules, trusted institutions and consistent risk
information will help communities, councils, iwi, insurers, banks and businesses
understand risks and act early.

Opportunity will:

- support passage of elements of the Climate Change Response Amendment Bill
that establish responsibility for local bodies to plan for the impacts of climate
change.
- extend the role of the Natural Hazards Commission to include assessing national
climate risk, recommending adaptation targets, coordinating open hazard data for
councils and iwi and hapu, triggering out-of-cycle updates of the national
adaptation plan, and working with homeowners, councils, insurers and banks to
identify highly vulnerable homes and funding resilience works or, as a last resort,
relocation.
- create a National Insurance Support Framework with national rules for identifying
and managing insurance retreat, transparent forward-looking risk assessments for

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 4

---

homeowners, and a fair cost-sharing model between central government, local
government, insurers, and property owners.

Resilient infrastructure

Climate adaptation is a national challenge that cannot be left to councils, communities
and households with vastly different resources and exposure to risk. Central government
must invest directly to coordinate action across critical infrastructure, share costs fairly
and fund prevention before disaster strikes, rather than repeatedly paying for recovery
afterwards.

Opportunity will:

- fund adaptation efforts with a $5b Climate Resilience Fund (see the
Intergenerational Infrastructure policy). $500m of the Climate Resilience Fund will
be co-invested in nature-based solutions to reduce emissions and make
communities more resilient to the effects of climate change.
- resource community-led resilience programmes through marae and community
groups, prioritising high-risk and low-income areas.
- require roads, bridges, rail, ports, and water systems to be designed (and when
necessary, built back better) to accommodate heavier rainfall and flooding;
upgrade or underground electricity networks; and, ensure water systems are
resilient to both drought and intense storms.

Resilient businesses

Ensuring businesses are aware of, and prepared for, climate-related risks means they will
be more resilient in the face of change, causing less disruption to their operations and to
the broader economy.

Opportunity will:

- support businesses to assess likely impacts (incremental, and major events) of
climate change.
- improve the resilience of our farmers by strengthening biosecurity systems for
climate-driven pest and disease risks; investing in rural water storage, shade
infrastructure, and heat-stress mitigation for livestock; backing research into
drought-tolerant crops, efficient irrigation, and regenerative land management;
and, supporting the rewetting of peatlands and restoration of wetlands – critical,

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 5

---

high-impact nature-based solutions that act simultaneously as carbon sinks and
as natural flood and drought buffers.
- ask the Reserve Bank to build on its climate stress-testing of banks by monitoring
the risks of mortgage lending exposed to flood and coastal hazard and insurance
retreat, and on commercial lending exposed to a rising carbon price.
- require transparent climate-risk disclosure for new developments, mortgages, and
insurance products so that buyers, banks, and investors can make informed
decisions and property markets are not destabilised by sudden shocks.

3. Lock in a long-term climate action plan
New Zealand needs a durable, credible climate framework that gives households, farmers
and businesses confidence to invest, while ensuring we meet our emissions targets at
the lowest possible cost. Opportunity will work to build political consensus around the
core architecture of climate policy, because businesses and households cannot plan for
the future when the rules change with every change of government.

Fix the Emissions Trading Scheme

Allowing carbon prices to be lower than they should be and giving free credits for large
industrial emitters mean the Emission Trading Scheme has delivered little real pressure to
change. Governments have also leaned on exotic pine plantation offsets: a strategy that
locks up productive land, harms biodiversity, and clogs waterways.

A well-functioning carbon price signal will influence strategic investment decisions that
will help us transition to a low carbon economy.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 6

---

Opportunity will:

- restore the integrity and impact of the ETS by implementing changes that create a
rising price path to drive decarbonisation across the economy and shift incentives
to reduce emissions at the source instead of relying primarily on removals.
- give the Climate Change Commission the power to decide annual ETS unit supply
settings, minimum NZU auction clearing prices, and cost-containment reserve
thresholds.
- build on the Assessment Framework for Carbon Removals released in November
2025 by developing a removals system that recognises nature-based carbon sinks
such as coastal and land-based native vegetation including wetlands.
- refine the forestry settings in the ETS to reduce forestry slash and
forestry-sourced sedimentation risk.
- increase the rate for the existing phase down of emissions-intensive
trade-exposed free unit allocations to arrive at zero before 2050, with an option
for current holders of free allocation to ‘cash in’ a portion to pay for capital
expenditure to transition off fossil fuels.
- implement a carbon border adjustment levy on imported cement in return for the
removal of free unit allocations and other subsidies from domestic cement
production.

Credible emission targets and budgets

Emissions targets define where New Zealand must get to, while emissions budgets turn
that long-term destination into measurable, achievable steps. Together, they hold
governments accountable and give households, businesses and investors the certainty
needed to plan and invest with confidence. To remain credible and effective, our domestic
budgets, international commitments and policies must form one coherent pathway.

Opportunity will:

- restore the link between our Nationally Determined Contribution and the Paris
Agreement 1.5 degrees goal and our national emissions budgets.
- develop a plan to meet New Zealand’s Nationally Determined Contributions and
record the cost as a liability on the Crown balance sheet.
- implement the Climate Change Commission's advice on amendments to the 2050
emissions reductions targets, including international aviation and shipping
emissions.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 7

---

Climate Resilient Aotearoa — Frequently Asked Questions

What is your position on oil and gas exploration?
Given the rapid expansion of cheap renewable energy and increasing pressure to
transition away from fossil fuel extraction globally, prospective investments in new
offshore oil and gas developments are now so unattractive that few institutional investors
are willing to countenance them. Our focus is on ending the Gas Security Fund that
artificially subsidises exploration activities.
We consider a reinstatement of the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration is probably
unnecessary. However, for the purpose of clarity, Opportunity would not oppose a
reinstatement of the ban on offshore oil and gas exploration should a future governing
party seek to progress it.

Will you reverse the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Act?
Yes. Tort law exists precisely because Parliament cannot foresee every new form of harm
and to stop a case currently going through the courts raises rule-of-law and
access-to-justice questions.

What methane reduction level does Opportunity Support?
In December 2025 the Government cut the 2050 methane target from 24 to 47% below
2017 levels to 14 to 24% below. Opportunity will restore a science-based target of at least
35 to 47%, as the Climate Change Commission advised, and will back farmers to get there
with proven technology, ecosystem payments and a pricing mechanism that starts only
when the tools exist.

Opportunity Party | Climate Action  Page 8
